title: ‘Percy Jackson’: How A Quest To Save Annabeth Makes Everyone Reevaluate Their Relationships In Season 3
full_text: Skip to main content By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine CMA Awards Hit 7-Year Audience High With Taylor Swift’s Return ‘From’ Lures Over 5 Billion Minutes Viewed In 3 Weeks After MGM+ Series Lands On Netflix Siegfried & Roy Series ‘Wild Things’ Gets Spring Release; Apple TV Teases Jude Law & Andrew Garfield As “Masters Of The Impossible” View All November 21, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Percy Jackson & the Olympians' Disney+ SPOILER ALERT! This post contains some details from the first two episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3. If there is one thing that the kids of Camp Half-Blood can count on, it’s that their lives are only going to get more complicated. Percy Jackson and the Olympians returned to Disney+ for Season 3 on Friday, and already the dynamics have shifted. The first episode opens with Percy ( Walker Scobell ) and Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) recruiting the recently revived child of Zeus, Thalia (Tamara Smart), to help them rescue two younger demigods — Nico and Bianca di Angelo, the children of Hades — and the tension is palpable. Related Stories Casting 'Afterlife With Archie' Disney+ Series Casts Its Archie, Veronica, Betty, Jughead & Sabrina News 'Gilmore Girls: A Year In The Life' Gets New Home On Hulu After Netflix Deal Ends, Release Date Set “I think that Annabeth’s presence is actually incredibly divisive between the two of them,” Smart tells Deadline of the dynamic between Thalia and Percy. Watch on Deadline In terms of sowing that division on screen, she adds that “a lot of it is based in our actual relationship in the best of ways.” “Walker also has the exact same personality and sense of humor. So, right right off the bat, we were definitely going back and forth and joking, and I think the only thing we had to do was just up the stakes and be serious about it, which was actually more difficult than we planned,” she says. Percy and Thalia can’t agree on almost anything, except their loyalty to Annabeth, who has unwittingly been thrown in the middle of their power struggle at the start of the season. So, when Annabeth is captured and brought to an enemy stronghold where she’s forced to bear the weight of the sky (the eponymous Titan’s Curse ), those two have to set aside their differences quite quickly. “She kind of kept them at a safe distance away from each other, because, as I guess we’ve seen the trailer, bad things happen when they’re not at that safe distance,” Scobell says. “So I think without her there, they’re forced to actually work together and try to figure each other out and attempt to understand each other.” Adds Smart: “They actually have to be forced into proximity to work together to get her back, because that’s their mutual interest. So, it’s really beautiful in a way that her absence brings them closer, which is a very human thing for us. I think as people, we’re just always brought closer by tragedy. But I think that for them specifically, a lot of ego has to get out the door for them to work together to achieve their mutual goal.” Rather than put a wedge in Annabeth’s relationship with either, Jeffries thinks that the tension between Percy and Thalia also provides some clarity for the daughter of Athena. Whether she’s ready to face that realization yet is another story. “I honestly feel like you get to see more Percabeth when it’s between Percy and Thalia,” Jeffries says. “I feel like her eyes open up a little bit. Annabeth is very smart. Even though she’s making it look like she’s not noticing, she knows [she’s developing feelings for Percy]. I don’t know if that’s more of like a denial between her of like, ‘No, no, I’m working right now. I’m on missions. I don’t have time to be falling in love…’ She continues: “You get to see the fight [in her] more, not physically, but just like ‘No, I love this person. title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Returns Lionsgate Franchise To Fortune With $120M+ U.S. Opening – Box Office Update
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Begins Global Weekend With $76M Running Cume – Update ‘You Can See Everything’: Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Crossing $100M Worldwide Tonight Derval Whelan Exits Searchlight As Head Of U.S. Distribution, Had 17-Year Run With Label View All November 21, 2026 8:25am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Zada in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Lionsgate/Everett Collection SATURDAY AM: Lionsgate has gotten The Hunger Games franchise back in the $100M+ opening territory that this Suzanne Collins IP is known for on the big screen as the sixth film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , is now posting a $120M North American start after a $56M Friday, which includes previews. In addition, the CinemaScore jumped from a B+ on the last film, Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, to an A- here. PostTrak exits have increased to an 80% definite recommend, and 93% positive. The pic is playing evenly throughout the nation, however, strong in South, South Central, Midwest and Mountain. PLFs and Imax are repping 47% of the weekend (15% Imax, 32% PLFs). AMC Lincoln Square is the highest grossing venue for the Francis Lawrence directed title at $168K. Sunrise on the Reaping as of now still has the fourth best opening in the franchise, but will likely be the third best, overtaking 2014’s Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 ($55.1M Friday/previews and $121.8M 3-day). The top two domestic starts in the Collins series are 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9M Friday/previews, $158M 3-day) and the original 2012 Hunger Games ($67.2M Friday/previews and $152.5M opening). Catching Fire stills stands as Lionsgate’s top opening at the domestic B.O. The entire theatrical marketplace is around $172.1M, just -5% off from a year ago when Wicked: For Good opened to a franchise best of $147M. With no Moana, Zootopia, or Wicked in the marketplace, there was some concern for a bit that we would hit a dry spell at the Thanksgiving box office, which would be unfortunate after a comeback year a the domestic box office, now coursing to $9B by the end the holiday with an eye at $10B by the end of the year. Thanks to Lionsgate, Sunrise on the Reaping is going to get us through. With Disney’s Hexed and Universal’s Focker-in-Law expected to post around $45M a piece over the Wednesday-Sunday stretch, it wouldn’t be shocking if Hunger Games takes the lead with $50M+ 5-day box office over that time as the franchise is typically strong over the Thanksgiving holiday. More… FRIDAY MIDDAY: Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is heading for the fourth highest opening for the Suzanne Collins franchise as of now with $110M stateside at 4,108 theaters after a Friday that’s $51M which includes those $21M previews. If the movie isn’t front-loaded, it has a shot at possibly becoming the third highest North American opening for the franchise. The industry overseas outlook is $97M, which if that holds means a $206.7M global opening. That latter number is not according to Lionsgate. A high $80M+ foreign start is within reach. Top Hunger Games openings at the North American B.O. belong to 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9M Friday/previews, $158M 3-day); the original 2012 Hunger Games ($67.2M Friday/previews and $152.5M opening), and 2014’s Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 ($55.1M Friday/previews and $121.8M 3-day). Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the Collins’ franchise, the fifth directed by Francis Lawrence. Altogether the previous five movies count $3.3 billion at the worldwide box office. Again, the jaw drop here is how this franchise turned its fortunes upward after hitting an all-time low in its opening three years ago with Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6M). Comps to other sixthquels are hard, and the opening jump between Songbirds & Sunrise is +147% — which is unheard of. The surge in domestic openings between Christopher Nolan’s Batman Begins and Dark Knight was +225%. Among all openings in November at the domestic B.O., Sunrise on the Reaping is currently 13th in a list of 16 movies that have bowed to over $100M for the month. RelishMix beams that the great word-of-mouth that the pic has “book loyalists showing up in full force, insisting this adaptation finally respects the source material. There’s trust running through the comments, ‘Director Francis Lawrence’s track record and the franchise’s unbroken prequel streak as reasons to believe this one sticks the landing,’ and, ‘We’ll need therapy after this,’ read as proof of the story’s emotional weight. Comments marvel, ‘Dang from Voldemort, Moriarty, Hades, and Ramses to President Snow, Ralph Fiennes catching literary villain roles like Pokémon.’ Others draw sharper comparison, saying ‘this is like the and/or of the Hunger Games I feel it, I know it, I read the book and they are going to break your heart.'” Overall social media reach is 652M across TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, X and Facebook which is not far from The Odyssey ‘s pre-opening reach at 680M and +66% above where Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes was in its social media universe, bowing shortly after the actors strike ended (393M). That 652M reach for Sunrise on the Reaping is 95% above other action-sci-fi-fantasy sub-genre features. “ Hunger Games cast activation index clocks 21 of 24 cast/creators activated with 40.4M total fans,” adds RelishMix in their weekly report. “Notably, Jennifer Lawrence and her newly rebooted Instagram with 9.2M fans activated a video from Fallon shot in an elevator at 30 Rock with 25+M views and 40+M views on the Fallon IG. Activations also include McKenna Grace at 13M, Maya Hawke at 10.4M, Elle Fanning at 7.7M, Josh Hutcherson at 4.2M, Glenn Close at 1.3M, Joseph Zada at 442K and Whitney Peak at 492K. As well, some cast-off-the grid, include Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Woody Harrelson and Kieran Culkin.” Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone in ‘ I Play Rocky ‘ Amazon MGM Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky from Amazon MGM Studios is looking at $10M in second place after a $3.9M Friday in its third frame 2,477 wide break and a running cume of $11M by EOD Sunday. The exits are excellent, so let’s hope there’s long legs on this Sylvester Stallone biopic which is 89% with Rotten Tomatoes critics and 98% with moviegoers. No. 3 goes to the second weekend of Paramount’s Johnny Depp Ebenezer at 3,545 theaters with $2.1M today, a 3-day of $8M , -58%, and ten-day total by Sunday of $32.8M . Fourth is Warner Bros’ The Cat in the Hat at 3,262 theaters, a third Friday of $1.7M, 3-day of $7.3M , -35%, and running cume of $47.5M . Fifth is the third weekend of Gkids/Toho’s Godzilla Minus Zero with $2.9M , -66%, after a third Friday of $700K at 3,000 theaters. Running total by Sunday is $54.7M . ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Lionsgate FRIDAY AM AFTER THURSDAY EXCLUSIVE: Lionsgate’s Francis Lawrence directed The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping came in with $21M in overall previews since Wednesday. As we told you, that’s the second best for the Suzanne Collins franchise behind Catching Fire ‘s $25.2M in 2013 and the second best for 2026 behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day ‘s $72M. title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Feasting With $120M+ in Franchise’s Box Office Comeback
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All November 21, 2026 8:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Joseph Zada and McKenna Grace in 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.' Murray Close/Lionsgate Logo text The Hunger Games : Sunrise on the Reaping has begun to ignite the box office . Lionsgate released the sixth film in the dystopian franchise in 4,018 North American theaters, and it grossed $56 million on Friday, including Thursday previews , as it heads for more than $120 million for the weekend. This would give it the fourth-best opening Friday in franchise history, besting 2015’s Mockingjay — Part 2 ($45.6 million) and 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($19 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9 million), 2012’s The Hunger Games ($67.2 million) and 2014’s Mockingjay — Part 1 ($55.1 million). Sunrise earned an A- CinemaScore from audiences, putting it below the A grades of the Jennifer Lawrence -led initial 2012 movie that kicked off the series and 2013’s Catching Fire but matching the A- grades of the two Mockingjay films. Related Stories Movies How 'I Play Rocky' Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood's Go-To Character Actors Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return The studio had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million , but other sources expected that it would collect between $100 million and $130 million, which now looks to be the case. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence ‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise in telling a story set 24 years before the events of the original 2008 book. This opening represents a major comeback for the series after registering its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , given that Sunrise on the Reaping is looking to open with more than double its launch. Starring Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer, Songbirds & Snakes — telling the backstory for the villainous President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes in the new movie — disappointed in opening to $44 million domestically for the weekend before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million. It earned a B+ CinemaScore, the lowest for the franchise. Joseph Zada and Whitney Peak in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Murray Close /Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection Sunrise on the Reaping holds a 67 critical score on Rotten Tomatoes as it lags behind the franchise’s first four movies but bests the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes . The new film has a 95 audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney wrote that it “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.” The movie opened the day after the launch of the hotly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto 6 , which does not appear to be preventing the film from thriving. Joseph Zada stars as Haymitch Abernathy, providing the backstory for the character whom Woody Harrelson brought to life in the first four movies. The cast for Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, Kieran Culkin and Maya Hawke. Among other weekend titles, Amazon MGM Studios expanded I Play Rocky to 2,477 North American locations after two frames in limited release. Peter Farrelly’s Rocky origin story earned $3.8 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, as it heads for an estimated $9.3 million. Starring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone, I Play Rocky landed a rare A+ CinemaScore, becoming only the second release this year to do so (after April’s A Great Awakening ). I Play Rocky holds an 89 percent approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 98 percent audience score. Rooney’s review described it as a “big-hearted movie about moviemaking, if not an artful one.” Anthony Ippolito and Stephan James in I Play Rocky. Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services In its sophomore frame, Paramount’s horror-tinged holiday offering Ebenezer is likely to claim third place with roughly $8.2 million for a decline around 57 percent to bring its domestic cume to $33 million. Johnny Depp marks his studio comeback vehicle with director Ti West’s reimagining of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol , which opened atop last weekend’s box office. Continuing to draw families in its third weekend is Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat , as the animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ classic children’s book is expected to gross around $7 million for a domestic total of $47.2 million. This marks a respectable decline of roughly 38 percent for directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni’s movie that features the voice of Bill Hader in the lead role. It is set to face fresh competition in the animated space from Disney’s Hexed over the forthcoming Thanksgiving frame. More to come. THR

title: Lindsay Hubbard Teases ‘Summer House’ Spinoff ‘In the City’ Season 2: “Better Than Season One”
full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All November 21, 2026 8:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lindsay Hubbard Charles Sykes/Bravo via Getty Images Logo text Amid filming season two of Bravo ‘s In the City , being a mom and her charitable efforts, Lindsay Hubbard is having a busy fall. Hubbard’s latest venture is partnering with No Kid Hungry’s Amplify Impact campaign ahead of Thanksgiving. The reality star served free breakfast sandwiches to New Yorkers at Give Back Bodega alongside season 21 Top Chef winner Danny Garcia at a pop-up event in Manhattan earlier this week. The campaign aims to help 10 million more kids access meals by 2032. “One in five kids faces hunger every day in the United States, and as a kid, they should just be kids. They should be playing and having a good time, and they shouldn’t have to think about where their next meal is coming from,” she told The Hollywood Reporter . Related Stories TV Melania Trump Stresses Humanitarian Efforts at Chic Premiere for Two-Episode Series Documentary Follow-Up Movies 'I Play Rocky' Stars Unite With Original 'Rocky' Producer for Film's 50th Anniversary Celebration The cause has taken on an even greater significance for Hubbard as a mother. Her daughter, Gemma Britt Kufe, turns two next month, and she explained how motherhood has changed her perspective on childhood hunger. “When I’m with Gemma, I have no nannies. I’m single mom-ing it hard,” she said. “I am spending my days feeding her, caring for her, making sure she’s eating. That’s the one thing that I’m always constantly thinking about. Even me growing up, I didn’t have to worry about where my next meal is coming from, so of course my perspective changes because it’s sad that we live in a world where one in five kids doesn’t have meals.” Lindsay Hubbard with Top Chef season 21 winner Danny Garcia on Nov. 18 in New York City. Courtesy of Give Back Bodega Hubbard’s transition into motherhood has also been documented on Bravo’s Summer House and its spinoff, In the City , which was recently renewed for a second season . While she remained tight-lipped about the upcoming season because the show is currently in production, she teased that fans will be satisfied with what’s to come. “We’re in the middle of filming it right now, and let me tell you, it’s got all of the elements of a great season two, better than season one,” Hubbard said. Page Six reported in October that the sophomore season will feature a cast shake-up. According to the outlet, new castmembers include Brittany Whitfield, Robert Morrison, Reagan Baker, Natasha Parker and Barthelemy Jallet. Meanwhile, season one stars Amanda Batula, Danielle Olivera and her partner, Eoin Heavey, as well as Andrea Denver and his wife, Lexi Sundin, will not be returning. Batula’s departure comes amid a particularly eventful period for the Summer House cast. She also exited ahead of season 11 of the original series amid the controversy surrounding her relationship with co-star West Wilson, who previously dated her close friend and fellow castmember Ciara Miller. Batula and her husband, OG Summer House star Kyle Cooke , had separated before the reports surfaced. Cooke was also close friends with Wilson. In alleged Instagram DMs, Batula cited intense online “hate” and “bullying” over her relationship with Wilson as her reason for not returning. Bravo has yet to officially announce the cast for In the City season two and did not respond to THR’s request for comment. Meanwhile, Hubbard herself has made headlines amid filming for the upcoming season. Earlier this month, Page Six reported that Cooke made out with Hubbard over Halloween weekend while filming a cast trip in Cancun, Mexico. The pair have been friends for more than a decade, and Cooke is also best friends with Carl Radke, Hubbard’s ex-fiancé and another OG Summer House castmember. Hubbard addressed the speculation with a laugh, telling THR, “No, Kyle’s like a brother to me. We just have a lot of fun, you know.” From left: Carl Radke, Hubbard and Kyle Cooke at Bravo Fan Fest in Charleston, South Carolina, on Oct. 24, 2026. Jessica Yurinko/Bravo via Getty Images With Summer House season 11 and In the City season two on the horizon, Hubbard isn’t expecting to step away from reality television anytime soon. “I’ll do it as long as they’ll have me on all these shows. I live a really big, full life that rarely ever stops. Things happen, and I have a lot to share at all times,” she said. “So until that stops, then maybe the TV portion would stop for me, but I don’t see that stopping anytime soon.” Also forthcoming is Hubbard’s memoir, Activated , which will be released May 18. Despite spending a decade on television, she said she still has plenty of stories she hasn’t shared with audiences. “I don’t need to rehash things that you can go back and rewatch,” she said of what readers can expect from the book. “So it’s all the stories that happen in life. I turned 40 this year, so you haven’t seen the first 30 years of my life. This is childhood, high school, college, my early PR days in New York, me living in L.A., me coming back to New York.” Hubbard added that she’s “actually really nervous” about readers discovering some of those previously untold stories. “I have been giggling and crying. It’s a lot of vulnerability,” she said. “I’m actually really nervous to open up some of these stories that people have never heard before, and it’s also the wildest moments of my entire life. There’s no holding back.” THR

title: Liz Daly Byrne, Model and Wife of PMC Vice Chairman Gerry Byrne, Dies at 81
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 8:10am PT Liz Daly Byrne, Model and Wife of PMC Vice Chairman Gerry Byrne, Dies at 81 By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest Liz Daly Byrne, Model and Wife of PMC Vice Chairman Gerry Byrne, Dies at 81 23 minutes ago How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change 17 hours ago Hearst Canvas Launches Frontier Collective Brand as U.K. Arm Builds Digital-Native Content Slate for YouTube 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Patrick McMullan via Getty Image Liz Daly Byrne , a model and philanthropist who was married to PMC vice chairman Gerry Byrne for more than 55 years, has died. She was 81. Byrne faced a battle with cancer three years ago, and recently learned that her illness had returned. She had faced recurring complications from severe injuries suffered in a bicycle accident in 2000. Byrne died Nov. 17 after a period of home hospice care in New York. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set Byrne was active as a philanthropist and social advocate through her work with the United Nations’ Operation Smile campaign, traveling internationally with the organization on medical missions. She had long been involved in causes to support military families and veterans. Byrne was remembered by her family, including her adult children, digital entrepreneur Gavin Byrne and actor Megan Byrne, as a woman who embodied “elegance, strength, wit, faith, generosity and compassion.” Byrne was also extremely fast on her feet, as she demonstrated in 1997 during the Cannes Film Festival. During a post-screening party for Warner Bros./New Regency’s buzzy period drama “L.A. Confidential” at a vineyard, a tipsy guest fell into the pool. As Variety reported, when Byrne saw what had happened, she “threw off her jacket and shoes and dove into the water for a dramatic rescue, after which she calmly took her seat for the sit-down dinner at fireworks show.” Born in 1945, Byrne grew up in the shadow of Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. She met her future husband Gerry Byrne — who served as publisher of Variety from 1989 to 2000 and at present is vice chair of Variety parent company PMC — while he was attending Fordham College in the borough. The two were neighbors, but in a wonderfully Bronx love story touch, Liz Daly met Gerry Byrne one evening during a ride on the D train. Early on, Liz Daly was drawn to New York’s fashion world. She signed with top modeling agencies Mannequin and Ellen Harth and launched her career as the primary designer’s model for top New York retailers Saks Fifth Avenue and Bonwit Teller. In addition to appearing in TV commercials, Byrne spent years as a runway model with Anne Klein, Donna Karan, Oscar de la Renta and Bill Tice. She then spent another decade working with renowned designers Bob Mackie and Ray Aghayan. Daly and Byrne married in 1969 at the chapel at St. Patrick’s Cathedral, after Gerry Byrne completed a three-year tour with the U.S. Marine Corps in Vietnam. In tribute to her husband’s service, Liz Byrne successfully launched a POW bracelet program to honor the sacrifices made by some families. The effort took root after being publicized nationally through coverage in the New York Times. Byrne was a dedicated marathon runner who participated in multiple New York City Marathons as well as runs hosted by the Marines in Washington, D.C. She was active in numerous nonprofits and in entertainment and media industry charitable efforts. title: Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 6:10am PT Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’ The film, which chronicles Egypt's fascination with professional lookalikes, premiered at the Cairo Film Festival By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’ 2 hours ago An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’ 2 hours ago Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be ‘Active’ in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’ 6 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Nehal Elkoussi The growing commotion on the streets near a soccer stadium would easily lead one to believe superstar player Kylian Mbappé himself was signing fan autographs. But, as seen in “ The Lookalike ,” the furore was not over the French player, but a charismatic impersonator. Premiering at the Cairo Film Festival , Nehal Elkoussi’s documentary follows three Egyptians who live in the shadows of their famous lookalikes: Mbappé; Egyptian singer and actor Mohamed Mounir; and late TV preacher Sheikh Mohammed Metwalli Sha’rawi. The doc trails the impersonators as they travel to meet fans, struggle to reconcile their personal and mirrored identities, and reflect on the impact a biological happenstance has had on their lives. The film is produced by Al Jazeera Documentary Channel. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set When asked about the inspiration for the project, Elkoussi tells Variety she grew up seeing Mounir impersonators, but was struck by stumbling upon one of her film’s subjects on social media and realizing he did dozens of concerts a month and had built a career around his resemblance to the star. “That was when the idea really clicked into focus: how do these lookalikes become a stand-in for the real star? What drives that? How do they draw in a big audience that sees in them a star within reach? What drives the audience that creates this kind of stardom for them?” The director first began developing the project in August of 2024, going on to film for eight months between 2025 and 2026. The experience of following the lookalikes and trying to understand people’s fascination with them came with several “surprises” for the filmmaker. “I was surprised by the smiles on kids’ faces in the streets whenever they ran into the Mbappé lookalike, reacting as if they were standing right in front of the real Mbappé,” she recalls. “I was surprised by how seriously the Mbappé lookalike took his work, and how committed [he is] as a content creator.” The Mbappé impersonator opened a fascinating avenue to “The Lookalike,” as the subject brought with him a whole roster of other soccer star impersonators, from Lionel Messi to Brazil’s goalkeeper Alisson Becker. This also allowed Elkoussi to build on Egypt ’s passion for the sport, and its growth in popularity in the Arab region following the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar. ‘The Lookalike’ Nehal Elkoussi Elkoussi also realized how class played a big role in people’s attachment to the lookalikes. “The poor needed a lookalike to stand in for the real star they can no longer reach,” she observes. “The people who go to a Mounir lookalike’s concert in a village in Gharbia, or the kids taking photos with the Mbappé lookalike in the street, or those seeking blessings from the El-Shaarawy lookalike, they don’t want a video on a screen. They need to feel that the star or figure is right there with them in flesh and blood, someone they can be near and talk to.” According to the director, this human warmth and connection is something “AI can never replace.” “On top of that is their seriousness and dedication to what they do. It’s a daily human effort, hard work, and an attempt to make people happy. It’s unlike technology, which just copies the surface and drains the soul out of it.” Premiering at home at the Cairo Film Festival has been a special experience for the filmmaker, particularly because her three subjects made it to the screening. “I made sure to share those moments with them as they’re the real makers of the film,” she says. “They really loved it, and they felt that we captured their lives and who they truly are without passing judgment or criticizing them. title: SkyShowtime Staff Complained About Workplace Culture & Handling Of “Racist Conduct” Before Comcast/Skydance Shuttered Streamer
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘MobLand’ Season 3 Starts Shooting As Season 2 Finale Drops On Paramount+ Gordon Ramsay Teams With ‘The Traitors’ Host Claudia Winkleman To Reboot ‘Hell’s Kitchen’ On ITV Kieran Culkin Reveals He’s Reuniting With ‘Succession’ Creator Jesse Armstrong On Movie View All November 21, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source SkyShowtime CEO Monty Sarhan has stepped down Getty EXCLUSIVE : Comcast and Skydance announced this week that they planned to shutter SkyShowtime for commercial reasons, but behind the scenes, the U.S. media giants have also been addressing serious unrest among employees at the joint-venture streamer. Deadline can reveal that a group of SkyShowtime staff lodged a formal complaint in June about the company’s workplace culture, citing concerns including favoritism, retaliation against staff raising grievances, and the handling of alleged “racist conduct” by an unnamed manager. SkyShowtime’s board, which is comprised of representatives from Comcast and Skydance, engaged external law firm Osborne Clarke to investigate. The board shared the outcome of the review with aggrieved employees this week, informing them that “appropriate action has been taken.” The response landed on the same day staff were told that SkyShowtime would be closed. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News CBS News Staffers Take Buyout Offers As Skydance Looks For Cost Savings News Biggest ITV Shows Like 'Love Island' & 'I'm A Celebrity' To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes A 50-50 pact between Comcast and Skydance, SkyShowtime streams in 22 European markets, boasting around 9 million subscribers. It is stocked with Comcast/Skydance series like The Day of the Jackal and Taylor Sheridan’s Yellowstone , as well as originals, such as Swedish drama Where the Sun Always Shines , starring Game of Thrones actor Kristofer Hivju . Deadline understands that SkyShowtime employee unrest had been percolating for months before the group complaint, with Deadline reporting in May that mood metrics had been below benchmarks. Some staffers also had misgivings about the amount of time CEO Monty Sarhan was spending in Philadelphia when he was running a business headquartered in London. At the time, senior SkyShowtime figures denied that morale was low and insisted that Sarhan was based in the UK. In their June complaint, around 25 anonymous employees raised at least five key concerns and questioned the leadership of Sarhan and Richard Thurston, SkyShowtime’s chief HR officer. Deadline has seen an email the employees sent SkyShowtime’s board earlier this month summarizing their position. “We have chosen to remain anonymous because of the nature of these concerns and because a previous employee who raised similar issues through internal channels was subsequently dismissed. Employees should not have to risk adverse consequences to raise legitimate concerns,” the employees said in their November 2 email. They listed their concerns as follows: “Inadequate responses to complaints of racist conduct by a manager; favouritism and unequal treatment of employees; promotion, levelling and compensation disparities influenced by personal proximity; selective resourcing and inconsistent treatment across functions; and retaliation against employees who have raised concerns.” They specifically questioned if Thurston was the right person to wind down SkyShowtime, arguing that employees must have confidence that decisions will be “handled fairly, consistently and transparently” at a time of “significant uncertainty about their livelihoods.” “We recognise the difficult circumstances facing the company. But a difficult transition is precisely when accountability matters most. We urge you to ensure that appropriate action follows and that employees can have confidence in the fairness of the process,” they continued. The SkyShowtime board responded to the employees this week. A board representative said: “As you are aware, your concerns were reviewed by an external law firm. The investigation has now been completed, the findings have been carefully considered, and appropriate action has been taken. “We take workplace concerns very seriously. To respect the privacy and confidentiality of everyone involved, we won’t be sharing further details. Thank you for raising your concerns and for showing a commitment to upholding SkyShowtime’s values.” Sarhan and Thurston are among the executives leaving SkyShowtime ahead of the business shuttering by late 2027. They have both stepped back from day-to-day operations and are on gardening leave. SkyShowtime’s position is that their departure is for commercial reasons and is unrelated to the external investigation. In an internal email this week, the SkyShowtime board thanked Sarhan for his “commitment and contributions.” Deadline offered Sarhan and Thurston the opportunity to comment through reps from Comcast and Skydance. Mark Neil, SkyShowtime’s CFO, will become interim general manager as the company winds down. Based out of Sky’s campus on the outskirts of central London, SkyShowtime employs around 300 people. Most of them will face an uncertain future, with employees in consultation about their jobs. Deadline first revealed concerns about the venture in May , when we reported that Skydance’s proposed ownership of HBO Max would put the David Ellison -run company in breach of its joint venture agreement with Comcast. Last year, Deadline revealed that the shareholders had ploughed $1 billion into SkyShowtime, even though it remained loss-making. Commenting on the external investigation, a SkyShowtime spokesperson said: “Concerns that were raised were reviewed by an external law firm. title: An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 5:50am PT An Iranian Woman Falls Pregnant to Avoid Execution in ‘Inherited’: Situation in Iran Is ‘Increasingly Complex’ The director, whose latest film premiered at the Cairo Film Festival, says geopolitical instability 'makes it harder and slower for new talents to emerge' in Iran By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Kylian Mbappé Impersonator Leads Colorful Roster of Doubles in Egyptian Doc ‘The Lookalike’ 2 hours ago Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be ‘Active’ in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’ 6 hours ago Robert Pattinson’s 007 Movie in Talks to Shoot at Pinewood as Studio Says ‘We’re the Home of Bond’ 7 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source A few years ago, Iranian filmmaker Morteza Alizadeh saw a photograph that he couldn’t shake from his mind: it showed mothers and their children going about their lives, which at first seemed routine, until the director realized it was taken inside a women’s prison. From that first glimpse into a little spoken-about reality, Alizadeh spent years researching how common it is for Iranian women to have children while waiting to be executed in prison. In “Inherited,” world premiering at the Cairo Film Festival , the director tells the fictional story of one of them, Mina (played by Mina Sadati). Sentenced to death for murder and running against the clock of her scheduled execution, she learns the only way to postpone her fate is to become pregnant. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set “My main goal with this film was to portray people who find themselves in difficult and sensitive situations, where they are forced to make choices to survive,” Alizadeh tells Variety . “These choices affect not only their own lives but, more importantly, the lives of others.” The director dedicated a long period to research, collecting an extensive archive of images from inside prisons, which included rare documentaries and footage from hacked surveillance cameras. He also spent months meeting and interviewing women who had been imprisoned and had either been released temporarily or were on leave. “With their help, we were able to design the entire prison environment in detail,” he notes. “Then our production design team recreated and built the whole prison set as closely as possible to the real thing.” By posing a complex moral conundrum when Mina’s family pleads with the unmarried prisoner to abort the baby to preserve the family’s honor, the director wanted the audience to “ask themselves” how much right “does one person have to decide another person’s fate.” “What gives us the authority to decide whether to take someone’s life or give another person the chance to live?” At the same time, it was important to me that the audience wouldn’t simply judge the characters for their choices, but would also try to understand the circumstances and the structures that put them in such difficult situations,” he adds. The film’s strong moral core and an unwillingness to offer easy answers speak to a long tradition of Iranian cinema established by names such as Jafar Panahi, Asghar Farhadi and Abbas Kiarostami. “I believe the roots of this cinematic tradition, of creating morally complex situations, can be found in Iranian society and its social and cultural conditions,” says Alizadeh. In that sense, the director feels a “deep connection” between “Inherited” and the work of his countrymen, which all come from a “shared reality of Iranian society” and are “influenced by the circumstances we live in.” “The experiences, contradictions and complexities of our society gradually build up inside us and find their way into our films, consciously or unconsciously.” Speaking of his home country, Alizadeh says the situation in Iran has become “increasingly complex.” “Alongside the difficult economic conditions that have created countless problems for people, to the point where simply getting through everyday life has become almost impossible for the majority, two wars in less than a year, people’s resistance against these attacks, and public protests between the two wars have made the situation in the country even more complicated.” “As a result,” he says. “It has become harder for artists to understand and respond to the social conditions around them.” This week, major industry names such as Mark Ruffalo and Tilda Swinton signed a statement shared with Variety that says they are “deeply concerned” by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Panahi, as well as the confiscation of his assets, the freezing of his bank accounts, a two-year travel ban and a two-year social media ban. “Iranian cinema is going through a very difficult period as it tries to redefine its relationship with these circumstances and overcome both internal obstacles, such as the relationship between filmmakers and society, and external ones, particularly censorship,” he goes on. “This makes it harder and slower for new talents to emerge. I believe the most important thing that can help move Iranian cinema forward and create opportunities for new filmmakers is their courage to tell stories while staying true to their own personal voice and style.” ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’ Director Says Finding Contributors Wasn’t Easy: ‘There’s Been a Landscape of Fear’ Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences ‘Grendel’ Animated Series Set at Netflix From ‘Widow’s Bay’ Writer Years After Live-Action Adaptation Was Scrapped ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Golden World Tour Sets 2027 Arena Dates Zarna Garg Sets Netflix Stand-Up Comedy Special (EXCLUSIVE) Maya Jama Strikes Deal With Netflix (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

title: Anthony Clark’s Official Cause Of Death Revealed
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Lincoln Center Theater Names Naomi Weinstock New Executive Director Of Development; Robert Jones Upped Anthony Clark’s Official Cause Of Death Revealed ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Broadway Review: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell & Jamie Lloyd Throw An Irresistible Party Of Shakespeare’s Great Comedy View All November 21, 2026 5:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Anthony Clark in 2003 Dan Steinberg/Getty Images An official cause of death for Yes, Dear star Anthony Clark has been reported: The comedian, who passed November 10 at 63, died from septic shock, with influenza A and chronic alcoholism also included as underlying conditions. Acute kidney failure is added as a significant contributing factor. The details comes from a death certificate obtained by People magazine late yesterday. The death of Clark, who started his career as a stand-up comedian and later became the star of TV sitcoms Boston Common and Yes, Dear , was announced earlier this month via a social media post from his Yes, Dear co-star and friend Mike O’Malley. Deadline reported at the time that initial reports indicated his death was connected to complications related to pneumonia and the flu. (Clark’s age has been variously reported as 62 and 63). Related Stories News 'Scream' Actor C.W. Morgan's Cause Of Death Revealed Obituaries Anthony Clark Dies: Comedian And 'Yes, Dear' Star Was 62 Clark was best known for starring alongside Mike O’Malley, Jean Louisa Kelly and Liza Snyder on the 2000 CBS sitcom Yes, Dear . Created and executive produced by Greg Garcia and Alan Kirschenbaum, the comedy about two couples living under the same roof ran for six seasons. Watch on Deadline On hearing the news of Clark’s death, Garcia, who also created NBC’s My Name I Earl , shared the following thoughts with Deadline: I’ve been very lucky to be friends with some of the funniest people in the world, and Anthony Clark had the most insane sense of humor of all of them. The things that would come out of his mouth were so unexpected and hilarious. Over the last two or three years we had reconnected, and I always looked forward to our monthly phone calls where we would catch up and make each other laugh. Recently, he was so full of joy and encouragement when he found out I was trying stand-up comedy for the first time. He enjoyed talking about the art of stand-up, being on the road, and would also offer some great advice. Just a few weeks ago we were laughing hysterically on the phone, trading jokes and telling stories. It’s a sad day, and I’ll miss him very much. I’m glad he was able to bring a lot of joy and laughter into the world. title: ‘Vengeance Is Mine’ Director Edwin Reveals Cast For ‘Dancing With My Shadow’ Based On Generation-Defining Album
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Jorrybell Agoto Dies: ‘Filipiñana’ Breakout Actress Was 32 Netflix Renews Unscripted Show ‘Physical: Asia’ For Second Season As Franchise Expands Georgia Lee Boards ‘Zhong Kui: Demon Slayer’ As Showrunner; Janet Yang & Simon Yam To Also Executive Produce View All November 21, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source First look of 'Dancing With My Shadow' cast Palari Films EXCLUSIVE: Indonesian filmmaker Edwin has revealed the five young leads for his upcoming feature, Dancing With My Shadow ( Menari Dengan Bayangan : Evakuasi ), inspired by the album of the same name from Hindia . Produced by Palari Films , the coming-of-age drama marks a return to youth-focused stories for Edwin following horror film Sleep No More (2026), which premiered in Berlinale Special Midnight earlier this year, and darkly comic action romance Vengeance Is Mine, All Other Pay Cash , which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno film festival in 2021. Based on the album by singer-songwriter Baskara Putra (a.k.a. Hindia), Dancing With My Shadow will star a mix of rising talent and familiar faces, including Rafly Altama, known for Riri Riza’s Rangga Cinta , and Hyori Mika, who stars in Palari Films’ recent Tokyo prize winner Jani Be Good . Watch on Deadline Related Stories Documentary Kate Middleton Documentary 'Heal' Set At BBC & NBC; Special About Princess' Three Peaks Challenge & Cancer Journey Gets Release Date & Trailer News Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days Also joining the cast is Muzakki Ramdhan, a former child actor from well-known genre films such as Gundala and Satan’s Slave 2: Communion , who already has more than 30 films under his belt. Newer faces in the young cast include Daffa Saputra, an actor and fashion model for whom this is his first significant film role, and Freya, a member of the JKT48 idol girl group, who started her acting career in horror hit Dominion Of Darkness and family drama A Brother And 7 Siblings . The cast is being revealed tonight at the final of the DBL Jakarta Series, Indonesia’s biggest high school basketball league, the world where the story takes place. Released in 2019, Hindia’s Menari Dengan Bayangan became the soundtrack of a generation, touching on subjects that young Indonesians rarely talk about openly: anxieties around growing up, pressure from home, and the fear of being left behind. It holds the record as the most-streamed Indonesian-language album on Spotify, and still regularly appears on the platform’s weekly Top Albums chart in Indonesia. The team behind the film explain that the album’s themes have been reworked into an original story, “with the music serving as an emotional map rather than a script”. Written by Winnie Benjamin, the story follows a quiet teenager, Agra, still grieving his father, who becomes the photographer for his high school’s rowdy basketball supporters club. Behind chants and chaos, he finds friendship, first love and a group of kids quietly learning how to survive. Produced by Palari Films’ Muhammad Zaidy and Meiske Taurisia, the film will be executive produced by Baskara Putra, Mira Lesmana and Dian Sastrowardoyo, with music by Petra Sihombing and Enrico Octaviano. Baskara will also appear in the film as himself performing on a concert stage. Commenting on the project he said: “This album feels like my own child. I’ve always wanted my albums to take on new forms, but handing it to someone else was scary. Then I realized the film shouldn’t be my life story. It should be a new story born from the same feelings. Edwin has always filmed young people honestly, without looking down on them. That’s what these songs needed.” For Edwin, the project marks a return to youth stories a decade after 2017 coming-of-age drama Posesif , which won a Citra Award for Best Director. “Agra spends most of the film behind a camera, deciding what to frame and what to leave out. I think that’s how many of us lived our teenage years,” Edwin said. “The stands are full of noise and bodies, but everyone there is carrying something they don’t talk about. I wanted to stay close enough to feel it.” Zaidy said: “From Posesif to Ali & Ratu Ratu Queens and Dear David , and now Menari Dengan Bayangan: Evakuasi , we keep coming back to coming-of-age stories. There’s always a fascinating crossroads in them. They feel familiar to so many people, yet there’s always a sense of liberation and empathy for people going through a transition in their lives. That stays relevant, even for adult audiences.” Dancing With My Shadow is being lined up for an Indonesian theatrical release in summer 2027. title: ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 4:45am PT ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’ 3 hours ago ‘Four Minus Three’ Takes Cairo Film Festival’s Golden Pyramid, While ‘Summer Meadow’ Wins Three Awards and ‘The Day of Wrath’ Nabs Two 18 hours ago Egyptian Actor Asser Yassin on His Dark Role in Psychological Thriller ‘Asal Ahmar,’ Alongside Hend Sabry: ‘I Like to Indulge in Intense Characters’ 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival For Iraqi-Swiss filmmaker Ali Toffan Al-Fatlawi , the idea behind “The Blind Ferryman” began with a thought that struck him during Iraq’s civil war in 2006. Living in Switzerland and watching the violence unfold in his homeland, he thought of two of his aunts who were blind and found himself wishing that blindness might spare his countrymen from the violence they were inflicting upon one another. That idea became the starting point for his fiction feature debut, which explores what it means to see, believe and trust our own perceptions. The film had its world premiere at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set “I think we lost the ability to think with our feelings,” Al-Fatlawi tells Variety. “Or, as we say in Arabic, ‘Seeing things with our heart.’” Ali Toffan Al-Fatlawi Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival Set in Iraq’s southern marshlands, the film follows Ayoub (Ahmed Moneka), a blind boatman who falls in love with Genya (Sam Rahmani), a mysterious woman whom nobody else can see. Convinced she exists only in his imagination, his community mocks him, forcing Ayoub to defend a love in which only he believes. “When you love someone, why do you need the agreement of other people?” Al-Fatlawi asks. “It’s your love, it’s your own decision.” The character of Genya draws on stories Al-Fatlawi heard from his father about a mythical woman who appeared to men in the marshlands, as well as ancient Sumerian mythology and the “Epic of Gilgamesh.” The filmmaker was particularly fascinated by the prominence of female deities in ancient Mesopotamian mythology, questioning how those figures gave way to the predominantly male image of God that characterizes contemporary religion. The marshlands themselves were equally important to his vision. Beyond their mythical associations, they offered Al-Fatlawi an opportunity to portray a side of Iraq rarely seen on screen, challenging the familiar images of war, poverty and destruction that have long dominated international representations of the country. “I don’t want to do a movie which shows that we are poor people, asking for sympathy,” he insists. “I’m really very careful not to make a movie which makes the West feel good about their life.” His determination to challenge preconceived notions also informed his casting. Ayoub is a Black Iraqi, while the threatening outsider who arrives from the city is a white, blue-eyed man dressed in religious clothing, a deliberate challenge to stereotypes about who looks like a hero and who looks like a villain. That tension between appearance and reality runs throughout the film, shaping everything from its characters to its visual language. A longtime painter and performance artist who later expanded into filmmaking, Al-Fatlawi developed the screenplay through drawings, often painting scenes before putting them into words. “I paint and then I write, I paint and then I write. That’s my way to write,” he explains. Working with his cinematographer, he chose the 4:3 aspect ratio to bring characters closer together within the frame, while composing wide shots that divide the image equally between the landscape and its reflection in the water. “I told him, I want really in the middle, 50%,” he recalls. “There is the image, and the reflection of the image in the water.” That same attention to perception shaped his direction of the actors. Al-Fatlawi instructed Moneka to keep his eyes open and fixed throughout the film, resisting conventional portrayals of blindness that might invite pity. “I don’t want people to feel sorry for you,” he recalls telling the actor. “I want you to be strong. You see more than everybody who has eyes.” For Rahmani, the challenge was to embody Genya as both a flesh-and-blood woman and a potentially mythical presence. Al-Fatlawi asked her to play the character as 50% real and 50% imaginary, a delicate balance they worked through in rehearsals and during filming. “I had to portray the whole spectrum without losing credibility as either,” Rahmani tells Variety. “Sometimes I went against my instinct, but that’s why I give so much credit to Ali as the creator of this whole world.” The experience was also a personal homecoming for the actress, who grew up in Jordan and Canada and had never lived in Iraq. After years of speaking Iraqi Arabic almost exclusively at home, spending nearly four months in the marshlands gave her the chance to use her native dialect freely, even in banal everyday encounters at supermarkets and restaurants. Rahmani says her time there brought her closer to her Iraqi heritage. “It was such a surreal and, I don’t know, special feeling full of relief,” she recalls. “I can only describe it as not having to mask all the time and code switch. I could just be myself.” “The Blind Ferryman gave me that gift, Ali gave me that gift of being more comfortable in my own skin,” she says. “It was healing for me.” The project began development in 2015, receiving support from the Doha Film Institute, El Gouna and Red Sea film festivals and participating in Cannes’ L’Atelier program in 2022. That same year, it secured approximately $2.5 million in financing. After a 45-day shoot in Iraq, however, Al-Fatlawi still had one crucial sequence to complete: an underwater scene he had envisioned years earlier. Rather than abandon it or spend an estimated $100,000 to $150,000 on a water tank, he found a cenote near Playa del Carmen, Mexico, whose submerged vegetation bore a striking resemblance to a painting he had made in 2021. Working with two underwater photographers who had never shot a feature film, he completed the sequence for a relatively modest $15,000. At CIFF, Al-Fatlawi says he has been particularly moved by audiences discovering meanings in the film that he had never consciously intended. “They add things which make the movie even richer,” he reflects. “They have the doors open. title: Obese Monkey Becomes a Weight-Loss Drug Guinea Pig in ‘Boltrim’ at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 4:32am PT Obese Monkey Becomes a Weight-Loss Drug Guinea Pig in ‘Boltrim’ at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar By Udita Jhunjhunwala Plus Icon Udita Jhunjhunwala Guest Contributor Latest Indian Auteur Girish Kasaravalli Looks Back on 50 Years of Cinema at IFFI Masterclass: ‘All My Films Talk About Othering’ 5 hours ago ‘Ramayana’ Star Sai Pallavi, Ravi Kishan’s ‘Spider-Man’ Anecdote, Grammy Winner Ricky Kej Light Up International Film Festival of India Opening in Goa 1 day ago Sundance-Winning ‘Cactus Pears’ Producer’s Delhi Beauty Salon Comedy-Drama ‘Nisa’ Bows at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Director Ashish Aryan is presenting “ Boltrim ,” a Hindi-English dark comedy about an obese monkey subjected to drug trials by a pharmaceutical giant developing a weight-loss injection, to the Co-Production Market at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar . The film traces the smuggled animal’s journey from Assam to a Delhi laboratory, exploring how far an operations manager at the trial agency will go to achieve the desired results. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set An NFDC Screenwriters’ Lab alum (“T for Taj Mahal”), Aryan has previously produced and written the web series “Matka King” (Prime Video), and directed “Roti, Kapda & Internet” (“Bread, Butter & Internet”). The idea for “Boltrim” came from a news report about a global shortage of laboratory monkeys, which had driven prices up to $50,000 per animal. “I was drawn to the disturbing intersection of two worlds – the smuggling and exploitation of animals in an increasingly lucrative clinical-trial industry, and our own obsession with bodily perfection, which a loss-making pharma company decides to capitalize on,” Aryan says. “Weight-loss injections meant to treat obesity and diabetes are now being widely used as a cosmetic shortcut. I want to explore how much cruelty we are willing to overlook in the pursuit of looking perfect.” The Writers Cloud, Jugaad Motion Pictures and Mirage Films are attached to the project, with $320,000 of its $1.2 million budget secured. Producer Siddartha Jatla (Busan title “Love and Shukla”) says the team is seeking international co-production and platform partners in Europe and Asia. The film is expected to enter pre-production in early 2027, with shooting planned for the first quarter of 2028. “If we find a partner at WAVES Film Bazaar, the timeline may change. Mirage Films has been part of three international co-productions, with collaborations involving China, the U.S., Taiwan, Indonesia, the Netherlands and Cambodia,” Jatla says. Producer Dheer Momaya of Jugaad Motion Pictures, whose credits include India’s Oscar submission “Last Film Show,” says he was drawn to Aryan’s determination and the story’s emotional narrative, which he describes as an “honest reflection of our times.” “It is challenging to raise finance for independent Indian films, given limited access to cultural and government funds,” Momaya says. “For ‘Last Film Show,’ we had Canal+ (France) come in with a distribution minimum guarantee and Stranger 88 (Belgium) with equity. We will explore similar strategic partnerships, as well as cultural and government funds in France, Germany and the Netherlands. We will also look at environmental conservation grants, as ‘Boltrim’ is a timely film about the dwindling natural habitat of humans and animals.” WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. title: Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 4:14am PT Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar 4 hours ago ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature 4 hours ago ‘Godavari’ Director Nikhil Mahajan Turns a Malegaon Carjacking Into Neo-Noir With WAVES Film Bazaar Project ‘Mongoose’ 14 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kharcha Paani Talkies Writer-director Garima Pura, a co-writer of the Oscar-winning documentary “The Elephant Whisperers,” is presenting “Nose Bone,” a dark comedy about a young woman from a Punjab border town scrambling to pay for an abortion, to the Co-Production Market at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar . On her 18th birthday, Tooti learns that she’s expecting and runs from the home of her abusive uncle to the closest city. With the legal deadline for a termination drawing near, she picks up odd jobs to cover the cost, working her way through a bleak job market and backstreet clinics before landing on the campaign trail of a local politician. Pura describes it as a film about allyship with minorities, solidarity among women and sexism that runs through institutions, one that asks what home can mean when the family inside it is abusive. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set Pura says she found that many women she met had been through abortions alone, for lack of money or support from family and society. “While there is institutional support, it is quite biased. Who gets to go to a public hospital and who can pay for it at a private clinic?” Pura is co-producing with Kharcha Paani Talkies. The budget is $262,510, with $65,000 in place, and the team is looking for co-producers, financiers and post-production partners, as well as the labs, grants and funds of the international artist community. Minocha plans a one-month shoot across Panchkula, Mohali and Chandigarh. “Brought up in Punjab and Haryana – India’s lowest sex-ratio states – I feel I have had front row seats of the lives of women there, and how they negotiate survival with their society – so that is also where the film is based,” Pura says. “That’s the world I know best.” Pura says she wants the film to bring into the open “the conversations I have had with women in living rooms, washrooms, boardrooms and in the waiting area of gynaec clinics.” Women, she says, cope with sexual violence “with grief, perseverance, impulsivity but most importantly – lots of dark humor – hence I’ve kept the tone of the film that way too. This film should be cathartic for women and hopefully informative for the uninitiated.” A Platform Busan alum this year, Pura has developed shows, films and documentaries for Netflix, Amazon Studios, JioHotstar, the British Asian Trust, USAID and Outlook Traveller. She is completing the Punjabi short “Kosi Sardi” (Are You Mad At Me), about two Punjabi women in their 80s, a tenant and her landlady, whose friendship breaks down. Minocha, a Mumbai-based producer who has worked with Mira Nair and National Award winner Rahul Chittella, heads Kharcha Paani Talkies, a film creation and curation studio, and is also producing a Kashish Grant-winning Punjabi film. She is a programmer at ALT EFF and a co-founder of DocNights by Bitchitra Collective. “I am a Punjabi woman too and I crave to see women from Punjab and Haryana center-staged. Across cinema – mainstream and indie – I find women being relegated to side-characters,” Minocha says, adding that the film dives into the inner world of a woman trying to make ends meet while facing a very real hurdle. “I also find a paucity of narratives where women occupy dark, dingy spaces and survive. ‘Nose Bone’ is a survival story and a fun one at that.” WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. title: NBC to Air Princess of Wales Cancer Charity Documentary
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All November 21, 2026 4:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Catherine, Princess of Wales Jordan Pettitt - Pool/Getty Images Logo text NBC will air a documentary special following the Princess of Wales as she completes a charity challenge to raise money for cancer patients. Heal: A Princess of Wales Special is set to air at 8 p.m. ET/PT Nov. 30 on NBC, a day after it premieres on the BBC in the U.K. The special will also at 11:30 p.m. Nov. 30 on Bravo and stream on Peacock starting Dec. 1. Heal will explore “life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness,” a description reads. Cameras followed Catherine as she completed the Three Peaks Challenge — climbing the tallest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in the course of 24 hours — in June in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. It will also feature the stories of other people facing cancer (the princess was diagnosed with a form of cancer in 2024 but was in remission as of 2025). “[Cancer] changes your body, it changes you physically,” Catherine says in a trailer for the special (watch it below). “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” All money from distribution of the special (it will also air in Australia on Dec. 1 and Canada on Dec. 7) will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and after a cancer diagnosis. Detail Films produced the special, with Benji Jackson directing. THR

title: Princess Of Wales Documentary ‘Heal’ Set At BBC & NBC; Special About Kate Middleton’s Cancer Journey Gets Release Date & Trailer

Heal , which will premiere on the BBC in the UK on November 29 and NBC in the U.S. on November 30, follows the Princess of Wales as she undertakes the National Three Peaks Challenge and reflects on her life as a cancer survivor. In June, Middleton completed the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours to support The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity. She had a crew filming her for the documentary, the existence of which had not been revealed until now. Vance & More In Heal , set against the backdrop of the challenge, Middleton reflects on her cancer experience alongside others who have faced major health issues, discussing the impact serious illness can have on the afflicted person and those around them as well as places and experiences that can help in the healing process while exploring life beyond diagnosis and recovery. Watch on Deadline You can watch a trailer below. It features Middleton’s brother James, who accompanied her on a climb, and her husband, Prince William, and children George, Charlotte and Louis embracing her at the end of the challenge. Prince William has done it a couple of times, tackling subjects he is passionate about with projects such as Prince William: We Can End Homelessness . He and his brother, Prince Harry, partnered on Diane, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy almost a decade ago. title: ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and ‘Uncle Joe,’ Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 3:59am PT ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and ‘Uncle Joe,’ Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest ‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’ 4 hours ago ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and ‘Uncle Joe,’ Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’ 4 hours ago ‘Four Minus Three’ Takes Cairo Film Festival’s Golden Pyramid, While ‘Summer Meadow’ Wins Three Awards and ‘The Day of Wrath’ Nabs Two 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source "Your Daughter" (Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival) For Egyptian filmmaker Sara Shazli , the camera became a way of asking her mother questions she had carried since childhood. Returning to Cairo from film school in Cuba, she would wait in the family kitchen, camera in hand, hoping to understand the woman whose devotion to cinema had so often left her feeling alone. “Was the camera protecting me from the answers she could give me? Was the camera a way of having her attention?,” Shazli wonders. With cinema occupying such a central place in her mother’s life, filming their conversations offered a way of reaching her through the very medium that had so often kept them apart. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set Sara Shazli Courtesy of Cairo Film Festival Those encounters became the foundation of “ Your Daughter ,” Shazli’s documentary about her relationship with her mother Marianne Khoury , the Egyptian producer and filmmaker who spent decades working alongside her uncle, renowned director Youssef Chahine. Premiering at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival, the film charts a daughter’s changing understanding of her mother, from resentment over her childhood absence to an admiration she had never anticipated. Shazli initially conceived the project as a search for Woody, the nanny who had helped raise her, hoping to reconnect with a figure who had played such an important role in her childhood. But as she developed the film and attended workshops with other filmmakers, their observations helped her recognize a more deeply personal story taking shape in the footage of her mother. “Someone told me, ‘Look at how you film your mother. You film her with so much love,’” she recalls. “It was actually painful,” she adds, because acknowledging that love meant confronting difficult questions, ones she had avoided for far too long. Those questions extended beyond Khoury’s absence to the expectations she passed on to her daughter. “I grew up with a mother telling me that you have to be independent from any man in the world,” Shazli says. “But it was so extreme. Why can’t both the dad and the mom help? Why can’t both be responsible?” Khoury had built her career while shouldering much of the financial burden and everyday demands of family life. Shazli admired her mother’s determination but questioned the sacrifices that came along with it. She sought a different kind of partnership, with a husband who shares childcare and financial responsibilities, rather than carrying those burdens alone. Her family’s cinematic legacy brought pressures of its own. Growing up around Chahine, whom she affectionately calls “Uncle Joe,” Shazli struggled to establish her own identity as a filmmaker. “Nobody put that pressure on me,” she says. “It was me, coming from that Chahine family, being compared to such a titan. What are you going to do with all this?” Studying film in Cuba offered distance from her family and from Egypt, helping her discover what she wanted to say as a filmmaker. “I started to see her differently and I started to feel for her,” Shazli tells Variety of her conversations with Khoury. She came to understand how her mother’s own upbringing had shaped the way she expressed affection. “It did hurt me to realize that she had grown up with a different kind of love, one where affection wasn’t always expressed through time and attention. She gave what she knew. You give what you receive.” Her growing empathy did not erase the hurt of her childhood, but it allowed her to see Khoury beyond the role of mother. Khoury, who took over Chahine’s production outfit Misr International after his passing, remains as devoted to her work as ever, but Shazli no longer sees that devotion solely through the lens of what she missed growing up. Becoming a mother herself brought another shift in perspective. “Now I feel like I really admire her,” Shazli says. “How on earth did she manage to do all this?” “That says a lot about her energy, about how much ambition she has,” she adds. “I’m nowhere near that, and I’m alright with that too. I’m actually happy that I don’t have that because you suffer when you have that. You want to be everywhere and do everything.” But that admiration does not mean she intends to follow the same path. For Shazli, whose earlier documentary “Back Home” explored her relationship with her father, filmmaking is also a means of working through deeply personal questions. “For me, filmmaking is really about healing,” she says. “If there’s no problem, there’s no film. If there’s nothing to discover, to heal, to dig deep into, there’s no film.” The Cairo premiere has brought an unexpected response, including from men who recognized their own family relationships in the film. “When somebody comes and tells you, ‘You made me want to speak to my mother,’ or ‘You made me want to speak to my father,’ that’s exactly what it should do,” she says. But having explored both parents on screen, Shazli is ready to turn toward fiction. “I did a film about my dad. I did a film about my mom. I’m done,” she says. “Now I want to have more fun. I want to write a fiction. I want to work with actors.
