title: ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature
full_text: × Nov 21, 2026 3:55am PT ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscar-Winning Doc ‘The Elephant Whisperers’ Co-Writer’s Dark Comedy ‘Nose Bone’ Follows a Punjabi Woman’s Race for an Abortion at WAVES Film Bazaar 4 hours ago ‘The Tree’ Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her ‘Italian Shoes’ Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature 4 hours ago ‘Godavari’ Director Nikhil Mahajan Turns a Malegaon Carjacking Into Neo-Noir With WAVES Film Bazaar Project ‘Mongoose’ 14 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source PIB French filmmaker Julie Bertuccelli , whose “The Tree” closed the Cannes Film Festival in 2010, said her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell’s novel “Italian Shoes” fell apart after a Canadian producer “stole the film” from her, and that she plans to shoot her next feature in India. Bertuccelli was speaking at “From Witness to Change: The Social Responsibility of Documentary Cinema,” a masterclass at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, moderated by Indian filmmaker Haobam Paban Kumar. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set Responding to an audience question, Bertuccelli said she set out to adapt the Mankell book five years ago. She wrote the script and cast the film, which was due to shoot in Canada, before the pandemic brought everything to a halt. “In fact there is a bad Canadian producer who stole the film from me,” Bertuccelli said. She did not name the producer and declined to give the full account. She said she was forced to cancel the project, adding: “I worked for quite four years, five years for nothing because they stole from me, they stole, you know, the movie and I could not do it. So it was very hard.” Bertuccelli turned to the directors in the room. “It’s a fight against you, against yourself, because you need to work, you need even when you are depressed or you have doubts, you need to continue, because the only thing that makes you a director is that you go on and you never, you know, you never stop your desire,” she said. She is now writing the new feature. It follows a French woman living in Mumbai who is slowly going blind and sets off on one last journey with her son, who is half Indian and half French. Bertuccelli plans to come to India to make it. “It’s my first time in India, but for so long I’m admiring your country, your culture,” she said. Bertuccelli is also finishing a second documentary alongside “The Violin Lesson,” which follows Rachel Routier, a violin teacher in Pantin, outside Paris, and is headed for French cinemas after airing on France Télévisions in September. She hopes to screen “The Violin Lesson” in Mumbai in the coming weeks, along with either “The Tree” or “Since Otar Left.” During two terms as president of La Scam, the French authors’ society for documentary makers, Bertuccelli created the Golden Eye documentary prize at Cannes, whose Indian winners include Payal Kapadia’s “A Night of Knowing Nothing” and Shaunak Sen’s “All That Breathes.” She also founded La Cinémathèque du documentaire in Paris, which hopes to stage a retrospective of Indian documentary. Asked by Kumar whether documentary carries a social responsibility, Bertuccelli said: “For sure there is a big responsibility because the film can change the life of somebody, you know?” She pointed to “School of Babel,” which followed a class for children newly arrived in France. The film was widely seen by school groups and shifted young viewers’ attitudes toward immigrant classmates, she said, and it helped protect such classes at a time when some were being closed. “Because I said with this film to all the Education Ministry: ‘So I made a film to show that France is great, but don’t touch it. Now you can’t destroy this,'” she said. Kumar later asked where cinema stands in the age of AI. Bertuccelli allowed that the technology can be useful for small tasks, such as sound work. “But I hate AI. Not just because, okay, it’s dangerous for us, we will forget how to have memory, how to think by ourselves. Also because they steal, they stole the film, you know, they stole the author rights. But also more because it’s an ecological, horrible, horrible thing,” she said. Documentary, she argued, is cinema’s last line of defense, because “there is a contract with you that when you see a documentary, there is reality, there is truth.” She added that “the 21st century will be the one of documentary.” Bertuccelli spent around 15 years as an assistant to directors including Krzysztof Kieślowski, Bertrand Tavernier and Otar Iosseliani before making her own documentaries. Her fiction debut, “Since Otar Left,” shot in Georgia, won the Critics’ Week grand prize at Cannes and the César for best first film. Her documentary work includes “School of Babel,” “Latest News From the Cosmos” and “Jane Campion, the Cinema Woman.” “The Tree,” starring Charlotte Gainsbourg, played IFFI more than 15 years ago, but Bertuccelli could not attend as she was eight months pregnant at the time. title: Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic – Doha Industry Days
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Al Hayba’ Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed ‘Caesar’ Biopic Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: “It’s Going To Be Good For The World” – Industry Days Doha Candle Media’s Kevin Mayer Says Company Caught Out By Drop In Streamer Demand: “We Didn’t See That Contraction Coming” View All November 21, 2026 3:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mohamed Mounir courtesy The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar . The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be unveiled. The project was announced at the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, just hours after the Qatari body gave an update on previously announced biopic Caesar , about Syrian whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan, announcing Taim Hasan as it star. Related Stories News 'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic News Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: "It's Going To Be Good For The World" - Industry Days Doha Mounir’s career spans nearly five decades across music, film and television. Watch on Deadline His 1981 breakthrough album ‘Shababeek’ established him as one of Egypt ’s most distinctive artists, with his work characterized by its fusion of Nubian folk and Arabic pop with Western genres like jazz, blues, and reggae. He is known to his fans across the Middle East and beyond as “El King” in reference to his 1998 album and play ‘El Malek Howwa El Malek’ ((The King is The King). Also working in cinema, his some 20 credits including collaborations with late Egyptian filmmaker Youssef Chahine on films including Egyptian Story (1982) and Destiny, which played in Out of Competition in Cannes in 1997 and was then selected as Egypt’s Oscar entry. Mounir was born into a Nubian family in a village in Southern Egypt, where he spent his early childhood. His family moved to Cairo, after the village was resettled due to the construction of the Aswan Dam in the 1960s, where his singing voice was discovered when he sang at a family gathering. The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir’s journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes. “Mohamed Mounir’s music holds a special place in the lives of audiences across Egypt and the Arab world,” said Film Committee at Media City Qatar Chair Hassan Al Thawadi. “ Bringing his story to the big screen is an opportunity to celebrate his artistry, the cultural heritage his work represents and its lasting social relevance, a story that connects generations of fans across the region and has the power to resonate with audiences around the world,” he continued. “This project also builds on our recent investment in extraordinary life stories from the region and reflects our ambition to develop a world-leading slate of biographical films that brings these stories to audiences globally.” Alongside the feature film, plans include a behind-the-scenes documentary featuring interviews with Mounir and those who have lived and worked alongside him, as well as documenting the development and production of the biopic. With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir. The Global South is a geopolitical and economic term that broadly includes countries in Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, most of Asia, and most of Oceania. Related Stories 'Logan' Star Dafne Keen Says 'I Was Offered Cocaine' as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman 'Made Sure No One Abused My Hours' on Set The Qatar Film Committee is an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub and is tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry. Founded in April 2024 by brothers Badie Ali and Hamza Ali, Chicago-based Watermelon Pictures has gained worldwide attention in its short time in business with releases such as Rashid Masharawi’s “From Ground Zero,” Annemarie Jacir’s “Palestine 36” and Cherien Dabis’ “All That’s Left of You,” which were shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar, as well as Kaouther ben Hania’s Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” The partnership between Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon was announced on the second day of the Doha Film Festival ’s Industry Days, which are running from Nov. 19-21. The plan is for the pact to spawn a slate of projects developed by Watermelon spanning comedy, television, genre and drama. Financial terms were not disclosed. “Combining Qatar’s commitment to world-class filmmaking, growing production capabilities, and investment in the creative economy with Watermelon’s access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and deep understanding of what resonates with audiences, the collaboration aims to produce commercially compelling films with high production values and international appeal,” the statement said. The plan envisions that these projects will shoot mainly in Qatar or be structured as Qatari co-productions. They will tap into the country’s growing production ecosystem and the Qatar Screen Production Incentive rebate offering up to 50% in cash, “creating opportunities for local crews, businesses and creative talent while strengthening Qatar’s position as an international production hub,” it noted. “Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world,” Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee, said in the statement. For Watermelon Pictures, the partnership marks a significant leap into larger-scale, mainstream production, backed by its distribution expertise. title: ‘Al Hayba’ Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed ‘Caesar’ Biopic
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Al Hayba’ Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed ‘Caesar’ Biopic Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: “It’s Going To Be Good For The World” – Industry Days Doha Candle Media’s Kevin Mayer Says Company Caught Out By Drop In Streamer Demand: “We Didn’t See That Contraction Coming” View All November 21, 2026 1:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Taim Hassan courtesy Syrian actor Taim Hasan ( Al Haybar ) has signed to star in Neon -backed biopic Caesar , about military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who risked his life to expose torture and human-rights abuses in prisons under Bashar Al Assad’s reign as president. At the same time, Ameer Fakher Eldin has been unveiled as the director on the drama. The Ukraine-born, Germany-based Syrian Lebanese filmmaker is known for films including Yunan and The Stranger . Bafta-nominated writing duo Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani ( The Mauritanian , Informer ) will write the screenplay. Related Stories News Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: "It's Going To Be Good For The World" - Industry Days Doha News Candle Media's Kevin Mayer Says Company Caught Out By Drop In Streamer Demand: "We Didn't See That Contraction Coming" Hasan has a big following across the Middle East and North Africa where he has built a career in Syrian, Lebanese and Egyptian productions, with notable recent roles including Jabal in hit organized crime drama Al Hayba and Mawlana . Watch on Deadline The signings were announced at a press conference at the Film Committee at Media City Qatar’s second Industry Days Doha, taking place within the framework of the Doha Film Festival , with Al-Madhhan, Hasan and Eldin in attendance. Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M , a key partner on the project, also joined the presentation. “The story of Caesar is not simply a story of suffering. It is not just the story of a photographer or someone who took pictures. It is a story about humanity. It is a story about confronting challenges. Above all, it is an ethical story. That is what we have worked to communicate,” said Al-Madhlan. “This was never intended to be simply a forensic or documentary exercise. It is a human story – the story of people who had lives, families and experiences, but whose lives unfortunately ended in inhumane circumstances.” The project was first announced at the first edition of the Industry Days Doha in 2025, with the Film Committee revealing it had acquired the life rights to al-Madhhan’s story and was partnering with Department M and Doha-based Katara Studios with the support of Kuwait’s Sard Media Group and Neon on board as a distributor. Syrian production company Tadmor Film City has also now joined the project to help with on the ground support. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented more than 650,000 deaths in Syria ’s civil war, which began in 2011, with an estimated 60,000 people believed to have died from torture in detention centers. Al-Madhhan was the Head of the Forensic Evidence Department of the Military Police in Damascus before fleeing Syria in 2014 with more than 54,000 images for the human rights abuses taking place in the country’s prisons. He spent three years smuggling evidence out via hidden memory cards inside his clothes and loaves of bread. Fearing for his life, he hid behind the pseudonym of Caesar only to unveil his true identity last year in the wake of Al Assad’s ousting in December 2024. The images he gathered were used to raise awareness around the brutality of the Al-Assad regime. His evidence also informed the bipartisan 2019 Caesar Act in the U.S., introducing sanctions targeting Al-Assad and his collaborators. “This project carries a tremendous responsibility,” said Hasan. “It is about the collective conscience of a nation and the individual experiences of people in Syria. I would particularly like to thank the team for approaching the story with such bravery and respect.” “We will tackle this project with the utmost care and sensitivity, working closely with my partners, Michael and everyone contributing to its success. As much as we want to portray the many different dimensions of Caesar’s story, we also want to show the beauty of Syria and the bravery of its people. We want to portray the real Syria,” he said. The Caesar signings are among a raft of announcements made by the Film Committee across the Industry Days, running from November 19 to 21 within the framework of the Doha Film Festival. Hasan received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the opening night of the festival.
